Europe Romanian health workers in national walkout over government health cuts Doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers across Romania staged a two-hour warning strike July 20. The action affected hundreds of hospitals and healthcare facilities between 9 and 11a.m., with only emergency services and around one-third of normal medical activity maintained. The SANITAS Federation members protest the government’s proposed salary legislation, which they say entrenches pay inequalities across the health sector. They also oppose a freeze on recruitment that has intensified already chronic understaffing. The health workers warn that the government’s austerity measures threaten both their livelihood and patient care. It is reported that an indefinite nationwide general strike will follow on July 28 if the government refuses to meet their demands. Ancillary staff at London hospital walk out over parity claims and union recognition Dozens of ancillary staff working in catering, cleaning and security for outsourcing firm ISS at Chase Farm Hospital in Enfield, north London began a three-day walkout on Wednesday. This follows a stoppage July 15-17. The GMB union members voted by a 95 percent majority for the action. They are seeking parity of terms and conditions with directly employed National Health Service (NHS) staff. They ae also seeking union recognition. Further stoppages are planned if there is no resolution. Strikes planned at UK rail company over safety fears Rail staff working for East Midlands Railway (EMR) are set to walk out on August 1 and the following two Saturdays. EMR runs express services from the East Midlands area of England to London. It also covers Yorkshire and the North West region of England. The Rail Maritime and Transport (RMT) union members plan the stoppages over safety fears following the introduction in April of a fleet of 810 passenger trains. Announcing the stoppages, the RMT said, “EMR has been sending trains into service that are likely to fail and require a full reset which leaves the train with no active safety systems including loss of communication between train drivers, dispatchers and trackside which has occurred at least three times in the last week alone.” EMR driver Shaun Burton was killed June 19 when his Corby to London St Pancras train ran into the back of a stationary train. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees has called for an independent worker-led inquiry to prevent another disastrous incident. Strike of housing association workers in London over pension attacks Staff working for the East End Homes (EEH) housing association in London’s Tower Hamlets borough were on strike Monday through Wednesday. They work as administrators, caretakers and housing officers responsible for around 4,000 homes. The Unison union members voted by a 100 percent majority for the action in June. They are opposed to plans by the housing association to move the workers from their current Defined Benefit pension scheme to an inferior Defined Contributions scheme. It would mean workers losing thousands of pounds a year pension income. Staff were assured their pension scheme would be protected when they were transferred from Tower Hamlets Council to EEH back in 2002. The staff, who held six days of stoppages in early July, are set to walk out July 27-31. Belgian firefighters in Brussels strike over staff shortages and poor working conditions Firefighters in Brussels, Belgium held a 24-hour strike from July 21, the country’s National Day, to July 22, protesting staff shortages, worsening working conditions and planned restructuring. The General Union of Public Services members oppose proposed staffing cuts, the removal of emergency vehicles, compulsory personnel transfers, changes to staff benefits and the introduction of an annual evaluation system, which they say will intensify pressure on already overstretched crews. The firefighters’ action follows strikes on December 31, 2025 and February 12 this year over chronic staff shortages. There are a shortfall of 200 full-time equivalent firefighters, while the number of call-outs is increasing. Firefighters insist that adequate staffing and resources are essential to guarantee public safety. Engineers for the Republic of Ireland Electricity Supply Board strike for overtime pay Around 20 engineers employed in the Engineering and Major Projects division of the Irish state-owned Electricity Supply Board (ESB) began industrial action July 15, imposing a ban on non-emergency out-of-hours work. The engineers are responsible for designing, upgrading and maintaining key electricity infrastructure across the Republic of Ireland. The Unite union members demand overtime pay commensurate with fellow workers on premium overtime rates. The engineers receive an “excess hours” allowance which was frozen from 2001 to 2025 and has conditions attached, which they say does not pay them for hours actually worked. The industrial action will remain in place until the ESB management addresses the disputed pay arrangements and the engineers' concerns. Middle East West Bank protest over planned school demolition Palestinian teachers supported by students held a protest outside their primary school in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 15. They were protesting plans by Israeli defence forces to demolish the school, which was built in 2016 and serves 190 students. Israel has carried out a series of such demolitions of Palestinian homes and infrastructure over recent years, often citing lack of building permits. Protests in Yemen over deteriorating living conditions Last week saw protests in several southern Yemeni governorates. The protests were in response to deteriorating service and economic conditions. In particular, they are protesting the costs and provision of basic services, electricity, fuel and water. Yemen has suffered years of conflict, leaving it one of the poorest countries in the Middle East. Protests in Iraq over power shortages Residents of the central Iraq city of Najaf protested Sunday against ongoing cuts to the electricity supply. They blocked the Najaf-Kufa road and marched to the governorate and provincial council headquarters. Iraq depends on Iran for around a third of the natural gas used in its production of electricity. The ongoing attacks on Iran by the US have impacted the supply of natural gas. The Ministry of Electricity apologised in parliament for the disruption to electrify supplies citing the regional conflict as well as aging infrastructure, lack of funding and rising summer demands. Africa Health workers in Mozambique extend nationwide strike Health workers across Mozambique have extended their nationwide strike for a further 30 days. They came out against the government’s failure to address longstanding demands over wages, working conditions and the chronic lack of medicines and medical supplies in public health facilities. The action called by the United Association of Mozambican Health Workers (APSUSM) continues as a total stoppage of work in health units across the country. Workers insist the crisis in the public health system is worsening. APSUSM said hospitals and clinics remain plagued by shortages of essential medicines, equipment and basic supplies, undermining patient care and placing impossible burdens on health workers. Union leaders say the government has failed to respond adequately to repeated complaints over deteriorating conditions, prompting workers to prolong the strike despite its impact on already overstretched health services. The extension of the strike underscores the deepening crisis confronting healthcare workers in Mozambique, where low pay, poor working conditions and chronic underfunding have fuelled repeated industrial disputes. The continuing stoppage shows the workers’ determination to fight for improved conditions despite mounting pressure from the authorities. Kenyan doctors in Kisii County begin indefinite strike Doctors at Kisii County Referral and Teaching Hospital have begun an indefinite strike after repeated delays in the payment of their salaries. This follows a warning issued by the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union (KMPDU). The industrial action has severely disrupted services, affecting outpatient clinics, specialist care and other non-emergency services. Doctors withdrew their labour over what they say is the county government’s persistent failure to pay them on time. The strike follows mounting tensions between the union and Kisii County authorities. In June, KMPDU warned that doctors would progressively scale back services if salaries were not paid by agreed deadlines, arguing that chronic delays had caused severe financial hardship for health workers. The union said repeated appeals to county officials had failed to resolve the dispute, leaving doctors no alternative but to strike. The Kisii dispute is the latest involving Kenyan health workers over delayed wages, staffing shortages and the failure of national and county governments to honour agreements. Healthcare workers have increasingly turned to strikes and protests as they confront deteriorating working conditions, while patients bear the consequences of repeated disruptions to already overstretched public health services. Congolese health workers fighting Ebola come under attack, continue their dispute over pay arrears More than a dozen attacks on health facilities and medical personnel have severely disrupted efforts to contain the rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ituri province. Treatment centres, burial teams and healthcare workers have come under attack from hostile groups, forcing some humanitarian organisations to withdraw staff from high-risk areas and limiting access to infected communities as the outbreak continues to spread. The deteriorating security situation has compounded an already deepening crisis for health workers. Medical staff have staged strikes over months of unpaid wages while working under hazardous conditions, with more than 100 healthcare workers infected during the outbreak. The violence, combined with staff shortages, insecurity and the absence of an approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has undermined contact tracing and delayed urgently needed care. The attacks reflect the broader social and political crisis confronting workers in eastern Congo, where decades of conflict, poverty and mistrust of the authorities have fuelled hostility towards the official Ebola response. International health agencies have warned that unless the safety of healthcare workers can be guaranteed and the necessary resources provided to combat the epidemic, efforts to contain one of the country’s worst Ebola outbreaks will remain dangerously compromised. Miners’ strike in Eswatini declared illegal Workers at Maloma Colliery in Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) began strike action July 13, after rejecting the company’s proposed two-year wage offer of a cumulative 9 percent increase—5 percent in 2026 and 4 percent in 2027. The miners, members of the Amalgamated Trade Union of Swaziland, blocked access to the mine as negotiations over pay broke down. The Industrial Court declared the strike unlawful after the company filed an urgent application, ordering workers to end the stoppage and cease obstructing access to the mine. Management demanded that workers get back to work before they would consider changing their offer. The court ruling underscores the growing together of the employers and the state in Eswatini and throughout Africa. The dispute reflects growing anger among miners over their declining pay relative to rising living costs. Egyptian paper workers hold sit-down strike over unpaid wages Workers at EMAK Paper in Egypt have continued their sit-in for more than a week, demanding payment of overdue wages and improvements to working conditions. Workers say management has failed to resolve their grievances despite repeated appeals, leaving them determined to maintain their protest until their demands are met. The dispute escalated as workers accused management of attempting to wear them down rather than negotiate a settlement. The action follows other labour struggles across Egypt, including strikes and sit-ins by textile, agricultural and other industrial workers over unpaid wages, low pay and worsening conditions, reflecting growing opposition to the impact of the country’s deepening economic crisis. Despite legal restrictions and intimidation, workers in a number of sectors have continued to organise strikes and sit-ins in defence of wages, jobs and basic working conditions. Union calls off strike by Phokwane municipal workers, South Africa A strike at Phokwane Municipality, South Africa has been called off by the South African Municipal Workers’ Union (Samwu). The municipal workers issued a memorandum of demands to the municipality June 19, accusing management of failing to address salary disparities, implement upgrade of the municipality from Grade 2 to 3, appoint interns, absorb contract workers and improve skills development. Concerns were also raised about the unsafe condition of the municipal building, which could collapse at any time. Workers said they had been forced to work in hazardous conditions without adequate safety equipment. They called for provision of personal protective equipment and appropriate tools. The strike disrupted refuse collection, with residents dumping uncollected rubbish outside municipal offices and spreading litter around the streets of Hartswater last week. On July 15, the Labour Court issued an interdict ordering an end to the strike. The court ordered removal of any locks or obstructions preventing access to the municipal building, closed since July 10. The court also barred Samwu members from further strike action, including picketing, but workers continued their action, saying they would strike until their demands were met. Samwu stepped in, calling off the strike after a meeting with management on July 20. The union agreed with management that “service delivery must continue,” ordering a return to work the following day. Management have issued timelines for the issues in the memorandum and committed to implementation of agreed actions, while deferring “some matters” to “a council resolution.” Subscribe to the IWA-RFC Newsletter Get email updates on workers’ struggles and a global perspective from the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Aslyum hotels are being closed, but where are people to go? Composite: Posed by models; Guardian Design; Tolga Akmen/EPA; Getty Images View image in fullscreen Aslyum hotels are being closed, but where are people to go? Composite: Posed by models; Guardian Design; Tolga Akmen/EPA; Getty Images First Edition newsletter Immigration and asylum Thursday briefing: What happens after an asylum hotel closes? In today’s newsletter: With more sites closed and more lives upended, a look at the rhetoric and reality of where asylum seekers should be housed Libby Brooks Thu 13 Aug 2026 01.44 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. This week, immigration minister Anna Turley announced, with minor fanfare, the government will stop using a further 13 hotels to house asylum seekers across the country. It brings the total shut this year to 44, in pursuit of Labour’s manifesto pledge, now reiterated by Andy Burnham , to cease hotel use completely by the end of this parliament. Doing so would remove what have become highly visible symbols of an increasingly toxic debate about migration. Less than 160 to go, according to the Home Office. There was a risk the announcement might be drowned out by howls of rightwing outrage after the prime minister dared suggest that middle-class areas also ought to house asylum seekers. “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers,” Burnham said. “I do believe all parts of the country need to play their part.” (In England , asylum seekers made up 0.29% of people in the most deprived local authorities, compared with 0.05% of people in the least deprived.) But what becomes of residents, protesters and communities after these hotels are emptied? I spoke to specialist reporter Diane Taylor , who has followed shifts in immigration policy and the individuals who must live through them for decades. First, the headlines. Five big stories Solar eclipse | Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north , going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out. UK news | Nurses are collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union has warned, as Andy Burnham promised to grapple with “the bigger questions” of climate adaptation. US politics | Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced. Science | Astronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object , a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light. Middle East | Israeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in the West Bank village of Qusra through a campaign of terror. In depth: ‘You can’t just magic away the intense protest and counter-protest and division’ View image in fullscreen An asylum seeker’s 12-year-old daughter, who uses a wheelchair and has epilepsy and a heart condition, is sleeping on the floor. Hotels were used as an occasional, temporary housing fix for asylum seekers pre-Covid, but became the default option in place of flats at the very start of the pandemic. The home office justification was public health – but I spoke to hotel residents back in 2020 who told me about cramped living conditions, limited access to food, drink and financial support, alongside spiralling mental distress. I still remember running through Glasgow city centre in June 2020 to reach the scene of a mass stabbing , and how my stomach dropped when I realised I was heading to a hotel housing asylum seekers. Badreddin Abdalla Adam Bosh, a Sudanese man, had stabbed six people including a police officer at the Park Inn hotel before being shot dead by police. An inquiry into his death is ongoing. To be clear: politicians across parties, support agencies and the far-right all agree that these hotels need to shut, though for different reasons. For the past six years – counter to the far-right “life-of-luxury” narrative – Diane has reported on life inside these hotels: rat infestations and food so abysmal it causes nutritional deficiencies. She has also exposed the vast profit made by private accommodation providers thanks to Home Office cash, such as Clearsprings, equating to £146 a minute over five years – yes, you read that right. What happens when a hotel closes? When a hotel closes, asylum seekers are moved – often at short notice – to houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs), former military barracks or other, usually more basic, hotels. People may have been living in the same hotel for years, and the new accommodation may be several hundred miles away, forcing people to re-build their lives – language classes, legal support, friendships – from scratch. Two barracks – Wethersfield in Essex and Crowborough in East Sussex – are now full, with planning permission being sought to turn three more into accommodation for asylum seekers: RAF Linton-on-Ouse, RAF Barnham and Bicester Garrison. Residents in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, close to Bicester, will – in an eccentric move – hold a referendum on seceding from the UK, in protest against plans to house more than a thousand male asylum seekers in the disused army barracks. The government estimates these new sites could eventually house about 3,750 people. According to the National Audit Office, barracks are not necessarily cheaper to fund than hotels, because of hefty set-up costs. The current estimated hotel cost per night is £144, compared with dispersal accommodation such as HMOs estimated at £23.25 per night. Although cheaper than hotels and barracks, there simply aren’t enough to meet demand; however Diane suggests “you also don’t get the same punishment optics with a rundown terrace in East Ham”. Some have found the transition gruelling. Huda is a 41-year-old engineering graduate who fled death threats in Tunisia with her two daughters, one of whom has serious health conditions. When their London hotel closed last month , the family were moved to another hotel that Diane describes as “extremely basic”. There are no facilities for Huda to cook for her children, and limited storage for essential medicines and equipment. When I asked Huda, via Diane, about this new accommodation, she described mashing up food with her hands so that her daughter can swallow it. Her daughter’s seizures have intensified since the move, she sleeps on the floor and Huda is painfully blunt: “My daughter is dying slowly.” Closures, protests and transformation View image in fullscreen Antiracist protesters outside the Bell in July 2025. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian Where asylum seekers go, far-right protesters often follow. Crowds of several hundred continue to throng at Crowborough every Sunday, and HMOs are now a growing target. Last Sunday in Kent, men in T-shirts bearing the logo “Christ is king” chanted “don’t unpack, you’re going back” outside an accommodation block in Broadstairs, rumoured to be earmarked for asylum seekers. And last week, over several nights of unrest in the Norfolk town of Thetford, crowds attempted to storm other suspected HMOs. Fifteen people were arrested. It’s worth noting that not every hotel has become a flashpoint. “It’s a mixed picture,” says Diane. “There are four asylum hotels near me, in a fairly middle-class area of London. Local residents and asylum seekers have lived together in a very low-key way, and I’ve never seen the slightest bit of trouble. “In the media, we always write about the extreme examples, understandably, but we don’t write about the hotels with zero problems.” The government claimed yesterday that closing hotels would have a transformative effect on local communities: “These hotels can once again attract visitors, support local jobs and drive footfall to nearby cafes, shops, restaurants and attractions, helping town centres and local economies thrive”. I put this to our resident Essex specialist Tim Burrows, who meticulously reported on a year of protests outside the Bell hotel in Epping. The Bell remains boarded up behind security fencing, with no apparent plans for reopening, and the effect on the community is clear: “While the closure of the Bell hotel has been welcomed by many in Epping, you can’t just magic away the past year or more of intense protest and counter-protest and the division that has caused.” The hotel, Tim says, “will long symbolise to one side of Epping ‘invader’ asylum seekers they blame for many of the UK’s problems, and to the other the concerning rise of far-right ethno-nationalist politics.” Where should asylum seekers be housed? The recent targeting of HMOs suggests that, as Diane tells me, where asylum seekers are housed is “almost irrelevant”. “There are people who don’t want asylum seekers here. If we put them in the sewers they would protest.” After Burnham’s comments about the distribution of asylum accommodation, Diane reminds me that there has been a fairly successful push to disperse people more widely in recent years “but, as the data shows, distribution is still not entirely equal”. It’s also the case that housing is more expensive to provide in middle-class areas. The government might also try changing the conversation to one that extends beyond houses, barracks and hotels to the people inside them. “Would it not be easier,” Diane says, “to ‘rebrand’ asylum seekers away from the scrounger, rapist stereotype into people who are grateful to be here and want to contribute any way they can – by doing work for the British community while claims are being processed.” Diane has written about some of the ad hoc volunteering initiatives already happening thanks to NGOs, but argues that having government in charge of them would mean wider and more efficient rollout. Better yet, says Diane: “Pay minimum wage for keeping streets clean, planting civic flowerbeds, growing free food for the whole area by tending community allotments. Deduct part of that to pay for accommodation. It would cut the cost to the taxpayer and boost integration.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen The discourse around Jason Arday’s departure from Cambridge is rooted in its own distorted reality. Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Alamy/Getty I spoke to Nesrine Malik about the Jason Arday story for First Edition last week . Her wider reflections in The Long Wave are as insightful as you’d expect. (And sign up here to read more from her.) Michael I felt utterly uplifted reading Natasha Walter’s considered, hopeful and very urgent challenge to feminists everywhere to reunite from the grassroots up. Libby After reading Peter Bradshaw’s review of the new Amy Goodman documentary, Steal This Story, Please! , I’ve booked a screening ticket. Michael It’s not only because we share a moniker that I’m enjoying Stephen Libby’s new fashion column . Here he writes about the sustainable joys of using your local dry cleaner to tailor vintage finds . Libby This exclusive by Sandra Laville is jaw-dropping given the temperatures, drought and fires we’re experiencing: just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff are working on climate adaptation. Terrifying. Michael Sport View image in fullscreen Paris St Germain’s Marquinhos lifts the trophy with teammates after winning. Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/Reuters Uefa Super Cup | After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg. European Athletics Championship | British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham. Cricket | Joe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side, telling his players to “be adults” after a string of late-night incidents. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “PM vows to tackle climate as nurses warn of heat toll”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Burnham prepared to spend more on housing asylum seekers”, the Times runs with “Firms’ fury at zero hours reform”, the Mail says “Rewilding link to record fires”, and the Express writes “Using stairs may cut risk of early death”. The FT ’s headline is “Ukraine ceases strikes on oil tankers using Russian port after Vance request”. On the eclipse, the Sun writes in its masthead font “The Moon”, the i Paper splashes “Once in a generation”, and Metro says “Here’s blot all the fuss was about”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Women in Afghanistan have been imprisoned in their own homes, unable to leave without male guardians; and barred from jobs and schooling. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The 21 million women and girls the world forgot Five years after the Taliban retook power, women inside the country explain how they have been silenced , while the Afghan journalist Zahra Joya asks why the world has looked away. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Getting the side-eye … Ioan Marc Jones tests out his hydration system. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Ioan Marc Jones has always hated running – he found it painful, boring and monotonous. But, an old football injury forced him to take up the sport properly. After conventional running advice failed, he turned to more unconventional tips from seasoned runners, including taking a shot of pickle juice, wearing nipple tape and listening to Hamlet. For the first time, Jones managed to run consistently for more than a month and discovered his own “running personality”. He may not love running yet, but he is enjoying the journey and, more importantly, starting to see himself as a runner. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/whats-o.text: Visits to the beauty salon are a luxury many of us enjoy, yet they can be rather costly. The alternative is a DIY home manicure, which in many instances doesn't last as long and lacks that polished, professional finish. Now, shoppers say they've been ditching the salons in favour of a mineral bond nail set from Australian brand Sistaco - and the retailer is currently offering a deal where beauty enthusiasts can receive three extra colours free of charge. Ordinarily retailing at £100.95, the set can be bought for £75 - roughly equivalent to the cost of two salon gel manicures. The set utilises a mineral bond applicator to deliver non-toxic, HEMA and TPO-free results in the comfort of your own home. READ MORE: People tired all the time say 'my energy is so much better' with 55p-a-day drops 'This £25 product changed the game for me' and it's now under £4 in Boots deal The brand promises buyers 'salon results at home from the first application' and claims the system removes effortlessly in just minutes. Those who despise waiting for their nails to dry will also be delighted to learn the manicure dries instantly, meaning no smudging for the more clumsy among us. The set has the potential to save regular salon-goers hundreds, or even thousands of pounds on their fortnightly appointments. Users simply apply a layer of base coat and set with an LED light, brush the powder onto the nail, apply a thin layer of top coat, before finally returning to set the look using the LED light once more, as reported by OK! For those whom the Sistaco set doesn't appeal to, LookFantastic is selling the Mylee The Midi Gel Polish Kit (worth £122) for £79 , featuring an LED lamp, four best-selling gel polishes and more. Meanwhile, those in need of nail tools might want to consider Sephora's £19.99 Manicure Tool Kit. The set includes a nail clipper, nail file, cuticle pusher, and a cuticle nipper. The Sistaco Mineral Bond Nail Set boasts an impressive 4.8 star rating out of five on the retailer's website. It also performs strongly on reviews platform Trustpilot, where devoted customers have awarded the company 4.5 out of five stars from thousands of reviews. One customer said: "Those compliments keep coming. I find in restaurants or cafes the girls/ladies who serve me always compliment my nails. Seems random strangers can't resist! They're always so impressed when I say I did them myself." Another raved: "Is this some sort of magic?! Love this kit and how easy it is to do at home, and it's long-lasting. Just past the two-week mark on the first mani and still going strong." A third said: "Goodbye to salons! This is 1 week+ and going strong. This system is so easy and convenient. I'm in love with the time and money savings. Thank you, Sistaco - 10 stars." It is worth noting that one reviewer mentioned experiencing some difficulty with applying the product at home, writing: "As a right-handed novice, doing my left hand was really easy, the right not so easy. I'm sure as I get more practice, my right hand will get a lot better. I also love the colour." Despite this, another customer praised the durability of the products in a Trustpilot review, writing: "Sistaco is BY FAR the best system/polish that I have ever tried! I am also very conscious of toxins and love that this is non-toxic! I also love that it last at least two weeks and can handle all the cooking, cleaning, hand washing, and childcare activities I do as a working mom!" A further reviewer on the platform stated: "Sistaco is spectacular. I've tried basic polish, gel, and dip powders, but nothing compares to Sistaco. I was hesitant to try yet another system, but I am so glad I did. "It's easy to apply, long‐lasting, and gentle on my nails. The colours are gorgeous, the products are high‐quality, and the community is incredibly friendly and supportive. I very highly recommend Sistaco Mineral Bond nail products."

https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: BERLIN — The trouble with Friedrich Merz is that when things get difficult , he can make them even more difficult. At a press conference this week , the German chancellor had barely begun addressing yet another disastrous set of election results when he stopped to rebuke a man moving in front of the cameras. “Haven’t you found a seat? Because you’re blocking the view for a lot of other people.” The icy tone was fleeting, but telling. In the face of crushing political pressure, Merz is trying to convince Germans that he can revive the economy, reform the welfare state, and halt the flight of voters to the political extremes, such as the far-right Alternative for Germany party and the Left party, both of which clinched victories in state elections over the weekend. Advertisement Advertisement Yet his combative public manner repeatedly gets in the way of the message. The irony is that the Merz I’ve seen away from the cameras can be engaging and capable of laughing at himself. His political problem is that too few voters ever see that side of him. Criticism of Merz’s manner is no longer just about style. His personal manner is cited as one of the reasons the Christian Democrats fared so badly in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: For the first time in the party’s postwar history, they failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering a state parliament. Aloof, confrontational and lacking in empathy — these have been frequent accusations as Merz has taken to the airwaves during the regional election season to fight his corner, sometimes making matters worse. One encounter earlier this month was particularly damaging. In a televised roundtable, pediatrician and influencer Bea Merscher attacked his record on health spending as “inhumane.” Merz angrily told her she was “going too far,” described doctors as “beneficiaries” of the health system, and added: “You are doctors. You couldn’t get by without this health system.” Fact checks found Merz largely right on the substance of health spending and reform — but he lost on tone. The public tends to prefer doctors to politicians in a bare-knuckle prime-time fight. “His problem is that he argues with opponents as though they are another politician or a board member,” a person who worked with him in opposition told me, confidentially, so as not to draw the chancellor’s ire. “He doesn’t think about how it looks from the sofa in front of the TV.” Advertisement Advertisement Yet there is another, more surprising Merz — one I have encountered over years on the international circuit, in brief conversations, small dinners and events where, once he loosens his tie, a more personable character emerges. When we first met, at a dinner in 2022 to discuss Germany’s laggardly response to the war in Ukraine, I pressed Merz — then opposition leader — on why he had not pushed then Chancellor Olaf Scholz harder to send longer-range weapons to Kyiv. His answer was evasive. Over a glass of Sekt afterwards, I risked saying so. It could have gone either way. Merz can end conversations sharply if he feels he is being treated badly. But he can also have a wry charm. He joked that I was being “very testing,” before explaining that he did not want to appear to be backseat-driving the government as the conflict intensified. Supporters participate in a Christian Democratic Union event in Berlin on Sept. 17, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images I had another go when our paths crossed at an Airbus factory in the U.K. in 2025, where he appeared with then Prime Minister Keir Starmer — who, to Merz’s amusement, called him simply “Friedrich,” an informality unusual in German politics. Again, Merz wavered on the sensitive question of supplying Taurus missiles to Ukraine. Again, I pressed him on the omission. He saw the funny side. “You again!” he observed the next time we met. There was another glimpse of that Merz when I asked whether he planned to congratulate former Chancellor Angela Merkel on her birthday. The question forced him into elaborate good wishes for the predecessor with whom he has had a famously testy relationship, after she bested him in the struggle for control of the CDU and, in his view, steered the party too far to the left. Advertisement Advertisement “Of course! We should all do that!” he replied — and laughed. These moments matter because Merz’s public image has hardened around a very different figure: formal, wealthy and remote from the instincts of many voters. A former corporate lawyer and BlackRock Germany chair, he has never made much effort to disguise the fruits of success in a country that tends to prefer its wealth worn with stealth. For years, that included his private plane and a taste for expensive cars. Since becoming chancellor, he has toned down the high life. Paradoxically, that may have made him appear more desiccated, not less: the Merz who is enjoying himself is often more engaging than the Merz who is trying hard to look chancellor-like. Merz’s instinct under pressure is to answer with more detail and more reform. A 34-point plan to revive Germany invited mockery for its complexity, while the AfD campaigned hard against his proposal to raise the retirement age to 67 and was rewarded at the ballot box. Now he needs to not only move faster, but also better sell his case: that state reforms will create new jobs and make pensions affordable in the future. Right now, many Germans think reforms will simply take something away from them. Andreas Rödder, a leading German political historian and Christian Democrat who once ran for chancellor, has long warned that Merz’s “firewall” against the far right would fail. He thinks the chancellor’s strategy of continuing and hoping the reforms eventually pay off is doomed. Advertisement Advertisement He argues that Merz lacks the courage to break with the Social Democrats and pursue reforms that are being slowed by tensions inside the coalition. Like others who have had on-off relations with Merz, Rödder also points to an oversensitivity to criticism and a tendency to discard people he has fallen out with rather than win them round. “Just saying, ‘I am staying where I am’ is not an answer here,” Rödder told me. “The question is why he doesn’t see that. He announces swathes of reforms and yet it is unclear how he can really deliver them in this coalition, so people stop believing what they hear.” It is, as Rödder puts it, a paradox: Merz had the courage and toughness to run for the CDU leadership three times. Yet the relaxed and self-aware Merz visible in private has remained largely hidden from the voters he now needs to persuade. He is a hard-working, pragmatic chancellor who knows many of the cues are suddenly uncertain, which the economic giant of a country needs. The question is whether he has the means and agility to learn what has gone wrong — and learn to speak to Germans anyway, winning over hearts and minds — when both have sorely deserted him. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Israeli settlers fly flags over a home they seized from a Palestinian family south of Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank in August. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images Labour ‘You were right’: Ed Miliband tells critics Labour was wrong on Gaza Foreign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’ Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor Mon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 03.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements. The foreign secretary will tell the Labour party conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy. He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel and Palestine about how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”. He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say. The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance on Israel and Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government. View image in fullscreen The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images Since becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank , which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions. The Guardian understands Miliband will say in his speech that the sanctions marked a definitive change in how Labour will approach the situation in the Middle East. “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right,” he will say. “And under Andy’s leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza . We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Labour shifts on Israel, but what difference will it make? – podcast Read more “We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements . We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed’.” Miliband will pay tribute to those who have campaigned against the Israeli onslaught in Gaza, though his warm words are likely to raise questions about whether the government will review the proscription of Palestine Action. Police arrested a number of demonstrators outside the conference hall on Sunday. “The bonds of solidarity between the British people and those who yearn for peace in Israel and Palestine are too strong to be broken,” Miliband will say. “Our decision to act mobilised the international community, country after country. This is how to make change happen in today’s world. Doing what is right and galvanising others to act too.” Miliband will say in his first speech to the party conference as foreign secretary that cooperation in imposing sanctions will be the beginning of a new bond with “likeminded countries” such as France and Canada, though it is also likely to be interpreted as being more willing to sideline the US. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has made an explicit argument for middle powers to do more to build alliances with each other outside traditional structures, and was direct in his desire to forge closer ties with and among European countries in a speech in Brussels earlier this month. A source close to Miliband said that would be a key theme of his time in office. “Britain’s interests are served by standing up for our values on the world stage. Our ability to build coalitions on big global issues depends on our ability to bring countries with us,” he will say. “This Israel/Palestine reset is a sign of how we want to do business. We are going to be propositional in bringing countries with us on the issues we really care about.” Explore more on these topics Labour Foreign policy Ed Miliband Labour conference 2026 Israel Middle East and north Africa Palestine news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://nypost.com/2026/10/03/world-news.text: Ten-day-old Kai Labban was the newest and tiniest star of Kibbutz Nirim, an idyllic cooperative oasis one mile from the Gaza border, when a nightmare shattered their world on Oct. 7, 2023. New parents Aimee and Uriel Labban were blissfully doting on their newborn baby boy when Hamas terrorists stormed their home and set it ablaze, trying to smoke out everyone inside. The Labbans’ sole focus was to save their precious, eight-pound, black-haired newborn, so they scrambled to their bedroom’s safe room and placed the tyke in the crevice of a windowsill. “I took the photo. I thought that if we don’t survive, at least the world will know we did our best to try,” recalled Aimee, who shared the image in real time with family abroad — who then sent it to the media. 3 Kai Labban celebrates his third birthday inside a kibbutz that came under attack on Oct. 7. Courtesy of the Labban family Outside, Hamas’ elite Nukhba unit stormed the kibbutz on motorcycles and pickup trucks, armed with automatic weapons and grenades, and set fire to civilian homes and cars and shot at them. At least one terrorist stood outside the family home with an RPG slung over his shoulder. Uriel held the door shut as the terrorists tried to yank the knob from the other side. Aimee said she doesn’t know why they never fired the RPG. Explore More Netanyahu fires back at Obama after he accuses Israel of stealing land, defends Palestinian terror Bizarre reason woman went overboard on a Royal Caribbean cruise ship revealed Cartel hitman earning $220 weekly claims he incinerated 250 people at Mexican ranch For nine hours, the family fought for survival after the terrorists moved on to other victims. The family was rescued by Israel Defense Forces troops, taken to an underground bunker and later to a hospital, where they were treated for severe smoke inhalation. Kai also developed blood poisoning and needed an oxygen tank for three days. “Even at 10 days old, he was a fighter,” his mom said. Meanwhile, Kai’s windowsill picture was already circulating around the world after extended family posted the heartbreaking image — which would go on to become an international symbol of hope as Kai became known as the youngest survivor of the Oct. 7 attacks . “We just tried to keep him alive,” Aimee, 33, told The Post on the near three-year anniversary of the savage attack that murdered 1,200. 3 Labban became an international symbol of hope and survival in the wake of the Oct. 7 massacre after a photo of him placed in the crevice of a safe room windowsill went viral. Courtesy of the Labban family “To me, it wasn’t his time,” she continued. “We knew he had other business to attend to.” As the heart-wrenching image went viral, support poured in from around the world. Well-wishers from Poland, Brazil, Greece and Russia sent expressions of love and support — notes reading, “Kai reminds me of my own grandson” — and gifts. “People asked what we needed,” recalled Aimee, adding that essential items like clothing, diapers, underwear, shoes and a car seat streamed in. “People have given us so much, but Kai gives so much hope and happiness to people.” In all, about 150 Hamas terrorists in three separate waves stormed the kibbutz — one of about 19 attacked that day — slaughtering five civilians and abducting another five, two of whom were killed in captivity. Though their home was completely destroyed, the Labbans, who both work on the kibbutz — Aimee as a teacher and Uriel as a hydrotherapist — were determined to return to their community. And they did, in August 2025. “This will always be our home,” declared Aimee, a teacher. “No terrorists will chase us out of our country.” Friends and family thought they were “crazy,” but Aimee insisted they return. “The message to Kai is, never give up,” she said. The parents think about what they will teach Kai about that fateful day that changed everything. 3 Uriel and Aimee Labban, with baby Kai, in Kibbutz Nirim on Oct. 1, 2023. Courtesy of the Labban family Though Kai was only a newborn during the onslaught, Aimee believed that “the mind and body have a record of something bad happening.” “It was the best of humanity alongside the worst of humanity,” said Aimee. “We survived people who wanted us dead and we saw people connect with Kai from worlds away.” As the family settles back into their beloved kibbutz of about 430 people, surrounded by its famous red wildflowers and dramatic desert backdrop, Aimee can’t help but feel flashes of the past. “Sometimes you think, ‘OMG, it’s going to happen again,’” said the mom. “But it still feels like the right place to be.” Aimee, who said both she and Uriel have been diagnosed with PTSD, will mark Oct. 7 by staying home and reflecting on all that was lost – and spared. “This is where we became a family, and this is where we’ll stay a family.” Trending Now in World News This story has been shared 2,028 times. 2,028 Netanyahu fires back at Obama after he https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/27/egyp.text: Egypt’s parliament on Monday authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military assistance to defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requests help, following a wave of attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.The House of Representatives said the decision passed with the required two-thirds majority. It allows el-Sisi, in coordination with Riyadh, to take measures to protect Saudi territory, sovereignty and holy sites against external attacks.Parliament’s statement did not specify what assistance Egypt would provide or announce that troops were being sent.On 17 October, Yahya al-Raei, speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, warned Egypt against military involvement, saying it would endanger Egypt’s own security and stability.El-Sisi said last week that any Egyptian military role would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, ruling out attacks on Yemen.The vote came as Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman joined Pakistani and Turkish officials for talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran. The Saudi foreign ministry said the visit aimed to open channels for negotiations and prevent further military escalation.Approval after three closed sessionsEl-Sisi first sought parliament’s backing on 17 October. MPs met behind closed doors on 18 and 19 October before postponing the decision until Monday.Deputy Speaker Assem El-Gazzar said nearly 500 MPs had asked to speak during the discussions. Most parties supported the request, but some lawmakers questioned the terms of a possible military mission.The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its MPs ahead of the vote to abstain. It said parliament had not received enough information about what Egyptian troops would be asked to do, how long they would stay, what the operation would cost or the risks they would face.While supporting Saudi Arabia’s security, the party warned against an open-ended military commitment and urged Egypt to leave room for diplomacy.The National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, had endorsed support for Saudi Arabia on 18 October. However, Egypt’s constitution also requires approval from two-thirds of MPs before its armed forces can be sent on combat missions abroad.Attacks continue as diplomats meetSaudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials in Tehran on Monday. Pakistan sent army chief Asim Munir, while Turkey sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.Fighting continues between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government.The Houthis said on Monday they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those claims.The Saudi-led coalition separately said it had intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh. It also said it had destroyed Houthi missile launchers and storage facilities in Yemen.The fighting threatens shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea and is part of the route to Egypt’s Suez Canal.Egypt’s main stock index closed 1.7% lower on Monday ahead of the parliamentary vote. Trading had been halted for 30 minutes on Sunday after the broader EGX100 index fell 10%.Saudi Arabia is a major political ally and financial supporter of Egypt. It provides aid, energy supplies and deposits at Egypt’s central bank.Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, mainly through naval operations. Its combat role was limited.
